title: FAST Entry Test: How the Analytical/IQ Section Actually Works
excerpt: The IQ section is the part of the FAST Entry Test that FSc coursework doesn't prepare you for at all. Here's what it's actually testing and how to build the skill from scratch.

content.text: Why this section catches students off guard

Every other section on the FAST Entry Test connects back to something you've studied for two years — Advanced Maths to your FSc syllabus, English to comprehension skills you've been building since school. The Analytical/IQ section is different. It isn't taught as a subject anywhere in FSc, which means most students walk into it with zero formal preparation and only whatever pattern-recognition instinct they happen to have picked up on their own.

That's exactly why it's worth taking seriously rather than treating as a "just wing it" section. Since it can't be crammed the way a Maths chapter can, students who start IQ practice late are usually the ones who underperform on it relative to their other sections — not because the questions are harder, but because they simply haven't built the pattern-recognition reps yet.
What "IQ reasoning" actually means on this test

In the context of entry tests like FAST's, "analytical" or "IQ" reasoning generally covers a cluster of question types built around finding patterns and relationships rather than recalling facts. The most common categories students encounter across Pakistani entry tests of this style include:

items: Number series (identifying the next number in a sequence)
Verbal reasoning and analogies (word relationships, odd-one-out)
Logical puzzles (seating arrangements, sequencing, basic deduction)
Non-verbal/pattern reasoning (shape sequences, visual pattern completion)

content.text: The exact mix and proportion of question types on FAST's specific paper can vary by cycle — the categories above are the general pattern-reasoning skill areas this kind of section draws from, not a confirmed breakdown of this year's paper. Verify against official past papers where available.
How to actually practice this, not just read about it

The single most effective way to build this skill is volume of exposure to varied question types under timed conditions — not reading explanations of "how number series work," but sitting down with 20-30 mixed questions and a timer, repeatedly, over several weeks. Pattern recognition is a trained skill, closer to how you'd build speed at mental arithmetic than how you'd learn a Physics chapter — the improvement comes from repetition, not from a single insight.

A useful habit is keeping a running log of which specific pattern types trip you up — if you notice you're consistently slow on logical seating-arrangement puzzles but fast on number series, that tells you exactly where your remaining practice hours should go, rather than treating "IQ" as one undifferentiated blob of difficulty.
Managing time pressure on this section specifically

Because IQ questions can look deceptively simple, it's easy to sink far more time into one tricky puzzle than it's worth, at the cost of easier questions later in the section. A reasonable habit is setting yourself a rough per-question time ceiling during practice — if you're stuck past that point, mark it and move on, then come back if time allows. This is a skill you build in practice sessions, not something you can decide to do for the first time on test day under real pressure.
Where this fits into your overall prep

If you're splitting study time across Advanced Maths, Basic Maths, English, and IQ, it's worth resisting the instinct to push IQ practice to "later" simply because it feels less structured than a Maths syllabus. Since every section on the paper is scored the same way per question, an hour spent turning a weak IQ score into an average one is often worth more to your overall aggregate than an hour spent polishing an already-strong Maths score by a couple of extra points.

Start IQ practice early, keep it consistent rather than saving it for a cram session, and track your accuracy by pattern type rather than by a single overall percentage — that's the difference between a section that quietly drags your score down and one that holds its own alongside the rest of the paper.

items.question: What kind of questions are on the FAST IQ/Analytical section?
items.answer: Common categories include number series, verbal reasoning and analogies, logical puzzles (seating arrangements, sequencing, basic deduction), and non-verbal/pattern reasoning. The exact mix can vary by cycle, so verify against official past papers where available.

items.question: Why can't I just cram IQ reasoning before the test?
items.answer: Pattern recognition is a trained skill built through repeated exposure over time, not a content area you can memorize quickly. Students who start IQ practice late tend to underperform on it relative to their other sections, not because the questions are harder, but because they haven't built the reps yet.

items.question: How should I practice for the IQ section?
items.answer: Work through varied question types under timed conditions repeatedly over several weeks rather than reading explanations. Keep a log of which specific pattern types trip you up so you know exactly where to focus your remaining practice time.

items.question: What should I do if I get stuck on a tricky IQ question during the test?
items.answer: Set yourself a rough per-question time ceiling during practice, and if you're stuck past that point during the actual test, mark the question and move on rather than sinking more time into it. This is a habit to build during practice, not decide on for the first time on test day.

items.question: Is it worth prioritizing IQ practice over Advanced Math?
items.answer: Since every section scores the same per question, turning a weak IQ score into an average one is often a better use of an hour than squeezing marginal extra points out of an already-strong Math score — especially since IQ can't be crammed late the way Math content sometimes can.
